Innovative Electric Propulsion System for High-Speed
Vessel Naruto
URI PEP Team
University of Rhode Island
Sam Miller, Ashley Sciacca,
Leonard Tourgee, Alex Lambert,
Shubham Chomal
March 22, 2025
Figure 1: Naruto (50)
1URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Contents
1 Background 3
2 Overview, Build, and Testing Process 3
2.1 Overview of Naruto . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 3

2.3 Power Storage . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 5

2.5 Propulsion and Pumps . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 7
2.6 Hull Construction Details . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 9

5 Future Plans 12

2URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Background
Figure 2: Naruto during sea trials
The increasing demand for sustainable and high-efficiency marine transportation has driven
the adoption of electric propulsion systems in both commercial and recreational vessels. As
part of this ongoing transformation, our team aimed to contribute a unique and practical
solution that blends proven electrical engineering concepts with forward-thinking naval architecture. The result is our vessel, Naruto, a compact, high-performance, electric-powered
boat engineered to perform in competitive conditions while reflecting modern design principles used in full-scale applications.
Electric propulsion offers numerous advantages, including reduced emissions, quieter operation, lower maintenance costs, and increased efficiency in specific speed regimes. Inspired
by the precision and flexibility of electric systems used in drones, RC vehicles, and unmanned
surface vehicles (USVs), we sought to implement a scalable solution that retains reliability
and performance in a dynamic aquatic environment.
Our design emphasizes not only speed and control but also maintainability and modularity, ensuring the craft can be quickly reconfigured or repaired in the field. The project was
approached with rigorous research into electric propulsion technologies, careful consideration
of mechanical and hydrodynamic factors, and a commitment to innovative problem-solving.
Overview, Build, and Testing Process
Overview of Naruto
Naruto is a 1/32 scale high-speed, unmanned, electric monohull designed by the University of
Rhode Island’s Promoting Electric Propulsion (PEP) team. The vessel’s hull form features a
three-stage stepped planing design that reduces wetted surface area at higher speeds, thereby
decreasing drag and increasing efficiency. This approach draws inspiration from performance
boats and offshore racing hulls known for their stability and maneuverability.
3URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Figure 3: Profile view of Naruto
The vessel is constructed using marine-grade wood layered with fiberglass and epoxy
resin. This method provides a durable yet lightweight structure capable of withstanding
repeated exposure to fresh and saltwater environments. The deck is segmented into watertight compartments, each accessible via uniquely fitted, 3D-printed, sliding hatches, and
supported by a skeletal substructure of aluminum cross-braces to enhance rigidity.
On the interior, the design reflects both form and function. Compartments are clearly designated for battery storage, electronics control, flotation foam, and scale-model cabin spaces.
This segmentation allows for simplified maintenance and effective balancing of weight, which
is critical for high-speed stability.
Vessel Specifications
Table 1: Vessel Specifications
Parameter Value
Scale 1:32
Full Scale Length 128 ft
Model Length 4 ft (48 in)
Full Scale Beam 48 ft
Model Beam 18 in
Hull Type Three-stage stepped planing monohull
Construction Material Wood frame with epoxy + fiberglass sheathing
Deck Design Reinforced with aluminum cross-bracing and epoxy bulkheads
Top Speed 21 mph (119 mph full scale equivalent)
4URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Power Storage
The power system is designed with modularity and redundancy in mind. Naruto supports
two primary battery configurations, enabling the team to swap packs depending on race
strategy, available charge, and endurance requirements. LiPo batteries were chosen for their
high energy density, reliability under load, and favorable weight-to-power ratios.
Figure 4: Mechanical room with batteries in place
Table 2: Battery Configuration Options
Configuration Voltage (Nominal) Capacity
2x 6S LiPo (in parallel) 22.2V each 28 Ah total
4x 6S LiPo (in parallel) 22.2V each 20 Ah each (80 Ah total)
XT90 anti-spark connectors are implemented to prevent damaging voltage spikes during
initial connection. Battery compartments are lined with dense foam and secured with Dual
Lock to prevent shifting under dynamic motion. Clear labeling and color-coded wiring
improve safety and speed during field operations.
5URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Figure 5: Measurement of the mechanical room opening (approximately 10 inches)
Control System
The control system for Naruto is built around reliability, modularity, and interference resistance. It features:
• A RadioLink transmitter and receiver system with active telemetry for monitoring voltage, signal strength, and operational status in real time. Also chosen for it’s
intuitive controls, ease of use, and simple reprogramming flow.
• A BEC (Battery Eliminator Circuit) to regulate a constant 5V power supply to
the receiver and lighting circuits, regardless of main battery charge.
• Signal wire isolation: The internal BECs built into the ESCs are disabled by removing the red signal wire, preventing voltage conflicts that could damage the receiver.
• A redundant circuit layout for critical systems to allow selective disconnection in
case of component failure.
6URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Figure 6: RadioLink controller connected to the Naruto system
All electrical connections are coated with epoxy and sealed with clear nail polish to ensure
durability in high-moisture environments. Wire routing prioritizes accessibility and heat
mitigation.
Propulsion and Pumps
Propulsion is provided by four Turnigy brushless outrunner motors, selected for their lightweight
design, high torque, and compatibility with programmable ESCs. Motor mounts are reinforced with aluminum struts and utilize adjustable pitch brackets for performance tuning.
7URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Table 3: Propulsion System Specifications
Component Details
Motors Turnigy brushless outrunner (drone-style)
ESCs (Outer Motors) Castle Mamba Monster X 6S (sensorless)
ESCs (Inner Motors) Castle Mamba Monster 8S (sensorless)
Max Current Draw 20A cruise, 40A peak (bollard pull) per motor
ESC Programming Castle Link USB software, throttle curve and timing tuned
Figure 7: Bilge pump in the hull of Naruto
Bilge management is handled by two peristaltic pumps located in the aft compartments.
These pumps are self-priming, debris-resistant, and can run dry without damage. They
are controlled through a brushed ESC with forward and reverse functionality, allowing for
automated clog clearing in operation.
8URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Hull Construction Details
Figure 8: Naruto during interior electronics installation
The hull is composed of multiple subsystems, each contributing to the overall performance
and durability:
• Fiberglass laminate layers on the exterior and interior protect the wood core from
water intrusion and physical stress.
• Reinforced bulkheads and aluminum square-tube cross-braces prevent flexing
at high speeds.
• Modular compartments support foam flotation, electronics, and aesthetic design
features like navigation lights and cabins.
• Sliding deck hatches made from 3D-printed ABS allow quick access to internal
components without requiring tools.
9URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Figure 9: Underside of Naruto showing rudder placement
The quad-blade propellers were chosen because they were cost-effective, accessible, and
reliable in testing. When tested against two-blade propellers of similar design, they were
found to produce less churn and froth, enabling a more efficient transfer of power.
Figure 10: Testing the hull for leaks in the fiberglass seal
Navigation lights, interior deck lighting, and nameplate LEDs are all integrated into the
structure and powered via dedicated receiver channels with pre-installed resistors for current
control.
10URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Modeling and Simulation
Our team employed a combination of CAD modeling and real-world empirical data to validate
and refine our design. The hull form was developed using Rhino 7 and Solidworks, enabling
us to fine-tune planing characteristics, balance, and structural layout before fabrication.
Figure 11: CFD Run showcasing drag and wake profile from a front view
Due to software limitations with Solidworks FlowSim’s free-surface simulation module, we
emphasized real-world testing backed by onboard telemetry. Castle ESCs log current draw,
throttle position, and error events, while GPS telemetry (via wearable sensors) allowed us
to compare performance profiles against expected values. Some CFD graphics may look low
quality as a result of having to completely redo CFD the day of submission after a technical
error.
Test data was gathered during high-speed lake runs and towing tank simulations. From
a 12-second data window at full throttle, we calculated a peak draw of 0.65 Ah/min per
motor, translating to roughly 39A. From this, we extrapolated the total required battery
capacity to complete a 2-mile run across several speed and load scenarios.
Performance Expectations
Based on our testing, Naruto demonstrates the capability to achieve a top speed of 21 mph
under optimal load and environmental conditions. The stepped hull provides stable lift at
planing speeds and significantly reduces slamming in choppy water, improving both battery
efficiency and component longevity. Our CFD runs also were validated by our real world
tests showing very similar charactaristics when on plane to the boat during testing.
11URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

Figure 12: CFD Run showcasing drag and wake profile from a side view when on plane
Figure 13: Click the image to watch our test footage
Throughout testing we found the boat to be capable of roughly 20 miles an hour for
12 miles of range on 2x 28Ah and 2x 22Ah batteries. The vessel is also capable of zeroradius turns using differential thrust and rudder control, a feature particularly useful during
obstacle or agility events.
In rough conditions, Naruto’s foam core and sealed hull design enable it to remain afloat
even when flooded. Testing has confirmed that the vessel can continue operating with partial
propulsion loss or minor hull flooding, increasing resilience during competitive runs.
Future Plans
Future iterations of Naruto may include:
• Additively manufactured hull and other critical components, such as prop shaft couplings, made from high-strength alloys.
• Integration of sensored ESCs to eliminate cogging during initial startup and low-speed
thrust conditions.
• Use of stainless steel bearings and waterproof connectors to further improve saltwater
durability.
12URI PEP Electric Propulsion White Paper

• Adoption of higher-pitch propellers for greater high-speed efficiency, tested against the
current configuration.
• A modular, solar-charging top deck to explore longer-endurance unmanned surface
operations.
• Enclosure upgrades using waterproof boxes for critical electronics, isolating motor control systems from navigational sensors.
Acknowledgments
As a team, we would like to thank our industry sponsor, PacMar Technologies. Their team
worked with us throughout the year in a collaborative and financial capacity.
Naruto’s design reflects the synthesis of hobbyist innovation and professional engineering practice. The propulsion configuration mirrors those used in high-performance multirotor drones, with independently addressable motors enabling precise control. ESCs are
programmable to match propeller loading and allow real-time telemetry logging, much like
systems in competitive e-racing vehicles.
Our hull geometry is inspired by commercial stepped-hull speedboats and incorporates
naval architecture principles in planing stability and structural reinforcement. Innovative
integration of LED lighting and bilge automation demonstrates practical foresight in both
safety and reliability—core features for any vessel operating autonomously in dynamic environments.
